# A Holiday for the Holidays · Ohio's Gas Tax Holiday · DNSC

> What you pay, what the state pays, and why gas costs this much: Ohio's 90-day gas tax holiday followed from your pump back to the price of a barrel.

Ohio's Gas Tax Holiday · From the pump to the price of oil

Oct 4, 2026 to Jan 2, 2027 · H.B. 519 · Gasoline and diesel

Free, from the public record

## A holiday for the holidays.

Ohio took its 38.5¢ gas tax off every gallon for 90 days. Start with your own tank, then follow the oil from your pump to the price of a barrel.

1 · Your pump

[Chart: A fuel tank, filled to your tank size]

### How big is your tank?

15 gallons

A choice (Fuel): Gas, Diesel.

A slider sets Tank size in gallons from 5 to 40, starting at 15.

A text field: What a gallon really costs, starting at $4.26.

A slider sets Price per gallon, tax included from 2.5 to 8, starting at 4.26.

Ohio's tax is a flat amount per gallon, 38.5 cents on gasoline and 47 cents on diesel, not a percentage. The price changes what you pay the station, not what the holiday saves.

A slider sets Fill-ups per week from 0.5 to 5, starting at 1.

This fill-up really costs

You pay

Ohio pays

Gold is what you pay. Teal is what Ohio's general fund now covers for you.

**For your business: vehicles, gallons, savings**

### For your business

A slider sets Number of vehicles from 1 to 200, starting at 10.

A slider sets Gallons per vehicle per week from 5 to 600, starting at 60.

A choice (Fleet fuel): Gas, Diesel.

Gallons in 90 days

Every week

All 90 days

Trucks that cross state lines pay Ohio's fuel use tax on the miles they drive in Ohio. The holiday cuts that tax too, so the savings follow Ohio miles wherever the tank was filled.

**Sources for this part**

- Ohio Legislative Service Commission, [Bill Analysis, H.B. 519](https://www.legislature.ohio.gov/download?key=28854) (rates: 38.5¢ gas, 47¢ diesel, to 0.01¢).
- Ohio Department of Taxation, [Motor Fuel Tax](https://tax.ohio.gov/business/motor-fuel-tax): "From 10/4/2026-1/2/2027 the rate for gas and diesel is reduced to $0.0001."
- U.S. Energy Information Administration, weekly [Ohio regular gasoline](https://www.eia.gov/dnav/pet/hist/LeafHandler.ashx?n=PET&s=EMM_EPMR_PTE_SOH_DPG&f=W) and [Midwest diesel](https://www.eia.gov/dnav/pet/hist/LeafHandler.ashx?n=PET&s=EMD_EPD2D_PTE_R20_DPG&f=W) prices (the default prices).
- Method: savings per gallon are the old rate minus the holiday rate (38.49¢ gas, 46.99¢ diesel); each fill-up assumes a full tank; a weekly habit repeats 90 ÷ 7 ≈ 12.9 times.

2 · The holiday

### Ninety days, October 4 to January 2.

Swipe the calendar →

**Day 1** of 90. 89 to go, through January 2.

[Chart: Calendar from October 4, 2026 to January 2, 2027 with Halloween, Thanksgiving, Christmas and New Year's marked]

Right through the holidays. Here's how it works at the station.

[Chart: A line drawing of a gas station]

- **The full cut, from day one.** Stations must pass the whole 38.5¢ to buyers.
- **They get back tax they already paid.** Fuel already in the ground tanks was taxed. Stations claim it by March 1.
- **Leftover tax-free fuel pays up later.** Fuel bought tax-free but sold after January 2 owes the tax, also by March 1.
- **The pump sticker can stay.** No new tax stickers required. Stations may update the rate on them.
- **Keep the cut, and the state can act.** It counts against the station's license and as a deceptive sales practice. The Attorney General enforces it.

**The details: what the bill says, word for word in plain English**

**The rate.** Ohio's tax drops from 38.5¢ to 0.01¢ a gallon on gas, and from 47¢ to 0.01¢ on diesel. It also cuts the fuel use tax commercial trucks pay on Ohio miles. Natural gas, propane and LNG are not affected.

**Who pays the tax normally.** The motor fuel tax is levied on fuel dealers (wholesalers, refineries and importers), and the cost is generally passed down to gas stations and then to buyers.

**Refunds.** For fuel already taxed at the old rate and sold during the holiday, stations apply to the Tax Commissioner by March 1, 2027, and are paid within 30 days from the Tax Refund Fund.

**Leftovers.** Fuel bought at the holiday rate and sold after it ends owes the difference, due March 1, 2027. A station can file both on one form so they net out.

**Stickers.** The state doesn't have to print new pump tax stickers. Stations may change the posted rate on them, as long as they don't damage the sticker.

**Enforcement.** Selling without passing on the full cut may count in the Tax Commissioner's licensing decisions and is an unfair or deceptive act under the Consumer Sales Practices Act. Only the Attorney General can enforce it; buyers can't sue on their own under this rule.

**Paperwork.** The Tax Department may delay its December distribution up to ten business days. October's report deadline moves from Nov 30 to Dec 7–15, 2026.

**How it passed.** H.B. 519 began as a car-theft bill. On Sept 30, 2026 the Senate added the holiday and passed it 26 to 5; the House agreed 78 to 16 the same day. Gov. DeWine signed it Oct 1. The federal 18.4¢ gas and 24.4¢ diesel taxes still apply.

- Ohio Legislative Service Commission, [Bill Analysis, H.B. 519](https://www.legislature.ohio.gov/download?key=28854), Sept 30, 2026.
- Ohio General Assembly, [H.B. 519 status](https://www.legislature.ohio.gov/legislation/136/hb519/status).
- U.S. Energy Information Administration, [federal fuel taxes](https://www.eia.gov/tools/faqs/faq.php?id=10&t=10).

3 · The auction

"Oil markets are essentially a global auction. The highest bidder will win the available supply."

*U.S. Energy Information Administration*

Swipe the map →

[Chart: World map of the oil flows in the story]

Canada and the U.S. to Ohio · Venezuela · Russia · Persian Gulf, about half blocked · Buyers bidding · Routes simplified

**Every refinery bids for the same barrels.** Oil sells on one world market, so a shortage anywhere raises the price everywhere, including Ohio.

**A fifth of the world's oil went through Hormuz.** About 20 million barrels a day in 2024. Since Feb 28, about half of that has stopped.

**Venezuela's oil changed course.** After the U.S. lifted most sanctions in January, Venezuelan crude to the U.S. rose from 137,000 barrels a day to 701,000 by July, almost all of it to the Gulf Coast. Ohio refines none of it.

**The Americas pumped more.** The U.S., Canada, Brazil, Guyana and Argentina add about 1.4 million barrels a day this year, far short of what's missing from the Gulf.

**Canada sells Ohio its oil, through a tense year.** The U.S. put a 10% tariff on Canadian energy in March 2025. Even so, 90% of Canada's crude exports still came to the U.S. in 2025, and Line 5 keeps feeding Toledo's refineries.

**Russia's oil found new buyers.** After U.S. sanctions in October 2025 and the Hormuz shutdown, India bought a record 2.6 million barrels a day of Russian crude in July.

**If the war ends: what changes, and how fast**

How fast prices come back

In 2022, the U.S. average for regular gas peaked at **$5.01** a gallon the week of June 13 and was back to **$3.09** the week of December 26, about six months later.

Pump prices tend to rise fast and fall slowly: crude moves first, and refiners and stations pass a drop along more slowly than a rise, in part because they manage their stocks through price.

A St. Louis Fed study found that an expected 1% rise in oil lifted gas 0.52% within a week, while an expected 1% drop lowered it 0.24%.

No one can promise a price. Here is what the record and the forecasters show.

Before the war, about 20 million barrels a day moved through Hormuz. By May it was under 10. If the war ends, it won't snap back overnight: the IEA says "a full recovery will not be immediate," because mines must be cleared and supply chains rebuilt, and it expects most of the rebound in 2027.

It happened once already · −52¢

In the three weeks after the mid-June deal to reopen the strait, Ohio's price fell 52¢, to **$3.56** on July 6. Prices had been easing since May on reports of a deal. The relief lasted about three weeks.

Same agency, two forecasts · 57¢ apart

In July, with the strait open, the federal EIA expected Midwest gas to average **$3.17** this October to December. In September, assuming the strait stays constrained through year end, it expected **$3.74**. Two forecasts under different conditions.

How fast it reaches the pump · 2.4¢

Each $1 change in a barrel of crude moves gas about 2.4¢ a gallon. About half shows up within two weeks and 80% within four. Pump prices fall more slowly than crude does.

How big is 38.5¢?

The gas tax holiday

**38.5¢**

Ohio, three weeks after the June deal

**52¢**

Between EIA's July and September forecasts

**57¢**

4 · The barrel

### The barrel sets the price.

Brent crude, the world's benchmark, the week before the war and the latest week. The holiday moves the pump 38.5¢; the barrel moves everything else.

### The price of a barrel

Brent crude, weekly, EIA

Before the war, week of Feb 27

$71

a barrel of Brent crude.

Latest, week of Sep 25

$117

a barrel. Up 64% since the war began.

**Why prices are this high.** Since the Iran war began on February 28, about half the tankers through the Strait of Hormuz have stopped. Ohio's gas followed the barrel, from $2.89 to a peak of $4.78 in May. The holiday takes 38.5¢ off the price; the rest follows the world oil market.

**Oil and pump prices, week by week, since 2020**

A deal in mid-June reopened the strait for a few weeks; it frayed in July, and the U.S. blockade of Iranian oil returned. Beyond crude, a gallon carries refining and retail costs and the 18.4¢ federal tax.

A choice (Time range): Since 2020, 2026.

Ohio · U.S. average · Brent crude oil · Iran war, from Feb 28, 2026

[Chart: Weekly Brent crude oil price and Ohio and U.S. regular gasoline prices since 2020]

Source: U.S. Energy Information Administration: weekly Brent crude spot price, and weekly retail regular gasoline for Ohio and the U.S. Gas prices are released every Monday. The war timeline follows EIA's [Apr 7](https://www.eia.gov/todayinenergy/detail.php?id=67424) and [Jul 15, 2026](https://www.eia.gov/todayinenergy/detail.php?id=67865) notes and its [September outlook](https://www.eia.gov/outlooks/steo/archives/sep26.pdf).

**Go deeper: where the road money comes from, where Ohio's oil comes from, what Washington did on diesel, and why diesel didn't come down**

The statehouse

### $725 million from the state's own fund covers the road money.

Fuel tax pays for roads and bridges. The state set aside money from its general fund, so ODOT, cities, counties and townships still get paid, on the months the tax would have arrived.

Swipe the chart →

[Chart: Money flows from the Ohio Statehouse to road budgets between December and February]

Set aside by the bill

$725M

From the General Revenue Fund, the state's main operating account.

Estimated tax not collected

$698M

The budget office's estimate for the 90 days.

Left in the general fund, June 30

$2.43B

Ohio took in $1.82B more in taxes than its budget expected last year.

**Ohio's surplus, in scale**

The general fund's money left over at year end, after bills already promised, was $2.43 billion. The rainy day fund held another $3.99 billion on June 30; spending it takes a vote of the legislature, and the holiday doesn't touch it. The $725 million is about 30% of the general fund's leftover. Counting everything, general fund revenue came in $981 million above the estimate.

**Every recipient, and your own share**

| Recipient | Estimated share of the $698.0M, 90 days |
|---|---|
| Ohio Department of Transportation | $373.6M |
| Highway debt payments | $73.1M |
| Ohio Public Works Commission | $16.8M |
| Ohio Department of Natural Resources | $6.7M |
| Ohio Department of Taxation | $1.5M |
| Turnpike Commission | $0.7M |
| Public Utilities Commission | $0.3M |
| Local governments | $225.3M |
| Municipalities (part of local governments) | $94.7M |
| Counties (part of local governments) | $81.6M |
| Townships (part of local governments) | $49.0M |
| Total | $698.0M |

"Your share" splits the state-paid part of your 90 days in the same proportions. About 65% of the first 28¢ of the tax goes to the state for transportation and the rest to local governments; of the part above 28¢, added in 2019, 55% goes to the state and 45% to locals. Spread across 88 counties, the counties' share averages about $927,000 each. The set-aside is $27 million more than the estimate; a separate $250,000 runs the holiday. Fuel tax reaches recipients about two months after the gas is bought, so a holiday from October to early January lands in road budgets from December through February.

**Sources for this part**

- Ohio Legislative Budget Office, [Fiscal Note, H.B. 519](https://www.legislature.ohio.gov/download?key=28857) ($725M item 110413 "Tax Relief Hold Harmless," $250K item 110414, $698M estimate, allocation table, timing).
- Ohio Legislative Service Commission, [Bill Analysis, H.B. 519](https://www.legislature.ohio.gov/download?key=28854) (the 65% and 55% splits).
- Ohio Legislative Budget Office, [Budget Footnotes, July 2026](https://www.lsc.ohio.gov/assets/organizations/legislative-service-commission/files/fy-2026-budget-footnotes-july-2026.pdf) and [Budget Stabilization Fund, July 2026](https://www.lsc.ohio.gov/assets/organizations/legislative-service-commission/files/infographics-budget-stabilization-fund-july-2026.pdf).

The refinery

### Ohio refines oil from Canada and the Midwest.

Four refineries turn crude into the gas in your tank. Almost all of it arrives by pipeline.

Swipe the map →

[Chart: Map of Ohio with its four refineries and the main pipelines coming in]

Refinery · Pipeline route, simplified · Utica shale counties

**4 refineries** Lima, two near Toledo, and Canton.

**607,000 barrels a day** About 3% of the nation's refining.

**98% by pipeline** From Canada through Michigan, and up from Texas on the Mid-Valley line.

**0 from the Persian Gulf** Every barrel the Midwest imported in 2025 came from Canada. None from the Gulf since 2018.

What's in a gallon, U.S. average, May 2026

Gas$4.48

Crude oil 52% · Refining 22% · Selling 15% · Taxes 12%

Diesel$5.60

**The refineries, and where the crude comes from**

| Refinery | Owner | Barrels a day |
|---|---|---|
| Lima | Cenovus | 183,000 |
| Toledo | PBF Energy | 172,800 |
| Oregon, near Toledo | Cenovus | 150,800 |
| Canton | Marathon | 100,000 |

EIA lists Ohio's crude sources as Canada, the Midcontinent, North Dakota, the Appalachian Basin, the Gulf Coast and Ohio's own Utica shale. Selling means distribution and marketing; taxes are federal and state together. Because the tax is a set amount per gallon, its share shrinks as prices rise: in 2025, at $3.10 a gallon, taxes were 14% of gas. Pipeline routes on the map are simplified.

Washington followed, for diesel

### On Oct 5 the federal diesel tax was deferred through Dec 31. Gasoline was not.

An executive order, "Emergency Tax Relief on Diesel Fuel," lets off-road dyed diesel be used on the highway and defers the 24.4¢ federal diesel tax on it for the rest of the year, with no interest or penalties, and tells Treasury to look for a way to forgive the deferred tax. It says nothing about gasoline, and it asks states to match it, which Ohio already has. The catch: dyed diesel is sold by farm and construction suppliers, and most retail pumps do not carry it.

**And for gasoline?** After Ohio's pause took effect, Sen. Bernie Moreno wrote: "Now it's time for the Federal Government to follow suit with a temporary suspension!" Here is what that would mean, from the record.

The federal tax is 18.4¢ on gasoline and 24.4¢ on diesel, unchanged since 1993. On a 15-gallon tank that is $2.76 a fill, on top of Ohio's $5.77, while both ran. When Maryland, Georgia and Connecticut paused their state taxes in 2022, 65 to 87 percent of the cut reached the pump, so about two dollars of the $2.76 would likely show up.

Every federal fuel-tax dollar goes to the Highway Trust Fund, which pays for roads and transit. A three-month pause was scored at about $10 billion in 2022. The fund already cannot cover itself: the 2021 infrastructure law moved $118 billion from the general fund into it, and the Congressional Budget Office projects it runs short again by 2028. A suspension means Congress backfills from general revenue, or the fund runs shorter. Ohio did the same in miniature, with $725 million from its own general fund.

It takes an act of Congress. The President said in May he intended to suspend the tax; bills from both parties have been introduced since.

**Sources for this part**

- The White House, [Emergency Tax Relief on Diesel Fuel](https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2026/10/emergency-tax-relief-on-diesel-fuel/), Executive Order, Oct 5, 2026; and the [fact sheet](https://www.whitehouse.gov/fact-sheets/2026/10/fact-sheet-president-donald-j-trump-promotes-diesel-affordability/) (dyed diesel on the highway; the 24.4¢ federal diesel tax deferred for the rest of the year, no interest or penalties).
- Yahoo News, [Ohio Senator calls for federal gas tax relief](https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/ohio-senator-calls-federal-gas-103000479.html) (Moreno's post, Oct 2026).
- Thomson Reuters, [GOP lawmakers, Trump push proposals to suspend federal gas tax](https://tax.thomsonreuters.com/news/gop-lawmakers-trump-push-proposals-to-suspend-federal-gas-tax/) (the 2026 bills; the May statement).
- The Bond Buyer, [Biden pushes federal gas tax holiday](https://bondbuyer.com/news/biden-pushes-federal-gas-tax-holiday) (2022: three months, about $10 billion to the Highway Trust Fund).
- Penn Wharton Budget Model via The Philadelphia Inquirer, [Your savings from a summer gas tax holiday](https://www.inquirer.com/news/gas-tax-holiday-summer-saves-penn-wharton-budget-model-20220624.html) (pass-through in Maryland, Georgia, Connecticut, 2022).
- Congressional Research Service, [Funding and Financing Highways and Public Transportation](https://www.everycrsreport.com/files/2023-05-24_R47573_2fdd993640445d646286ecfe0df6cc5570d409a6.html) ($118 billion general-fund transfer under the 2021 law; 2028 shortfall).

Two stations, October 2026

### Why diesel didn't come down.

[Image: A Wawa price sign: ethanol free $4.36, diesel $6.21, regular $3.36.]

Wawa · photographed by the author, October 2026

[Image: A Thorntons price sign at Tylersville Road: unleaded $3.49, diesel $6.09.]

Thorntons at Tylersville Road · photographed by the author, October 2026

Diesel costs $2.85 more than regular at one station and $2.60 more at the other, about $2.70 a gallon on fuels from the same barrel. The tax holiday is not the gap: Ohio took 38.5¢ off gasoline and 47¢ off diesel.

**The pool is low.** Diesel and heating oil come from the same pool of fuel, called distillate. U.S. distillate stocks have been below their five-year range since April. The last week of September they stood at 105.2 million barrels, 18.4 million less than a year earlier, and the Energy Information Administration expects them to stay below the five-year low through most of 2027.

**Supply was pulled three ways.** The Iran war cut the distillate that Middle East refineries ship. Ukraine has struck Russian refineries at least 100 times since August 2025; in July Russia banned diesel exports, and they fell by nearly half. With the world short, U.S. refiners sell more abroad: U.S. net exports of distillate have been near or above their five-year high every month since February.

**Refiners earn more on diesel.** The week of September 21, a gallon of diesel sold wholesale in New York Harbor for $2.17 more than the Brent crude it came from. A gallon of gasoline sold for 79¢ more. EIA expects diesel's margin to stay above $2 a gallon from August through November. The national average for diesel reached $6.53 that week, the highest in EIA's weekly series, which begins in 1994; this week it is $6.20. Heating-oil season draws on the same pool.

**Sources for this part**

- U.S. Energy Information Administration, [Short-Term Energy Outlook, September 2026](https://www.eia.gov/outlooks/steo/archives/sep26.pdf), U.S. Petroleum Products (distillate below the five-year range since April and below the five-year low through most of 2027; lost supply from the Middle East, Russia and China; net exports near or above the five-year high since February; diesel crack spreads above $2 a gallon August through November; heating oil).
- EIA, [Weekly U.S. ending stocks of distillate fuel oil](https://www.eia.gov/dnav/pet/hist/LeafHandler.ashx?n=PET&s=WDISTUS1&f=W), from the Weekly Petroleum Status Report (105.2 million barrels the week ending Sep 25, 2026; 123.6 million a year earlier).
- Oil & Gas Journal, [Falling Russian diesel exports tighten global distillate markets](https://www.ogj.com/general-interest/economics-markets/news/55391756/falling-russian-diesel-exports-tighten-global-distillate-markets), Jul 17, 2026 (at least 100 strikes on Russian refineries since August 2025; the export ban; exports down nearly half).
- EIA spot prices, [New York Harbor ultra-low-sulfur diesel](https://www.eia.gov/dnav/pet/hist/LeafHandler.ashx?n=PET&s=EER_EPD2DXL0_PF4_Y35NY_DPG&f=D), [New York Harbor conventional gasoline](https://www.eia.gov/dnav/pet/hist/LeafHandler.ashx?n=PET&s=EER_EPMRU_PF4_Y35NY_DPG&f=D) and [Brent crude](https://www.eia.gov/dnav/pet/hist/LeafHandler.ashx?n=PET&s=RBRTE&f=D), daily, Sep 21 to 25, 2026 (week averages: diesel $4.96, gasoline $3.58, Brent $117.08 a barrel, or $2.79 a gallon).
- EIA, [Weekly U.S. on-highway diesel retail price](https://www.eia.gov/dnav/pet/hist/LeafHandler.ashx?n=PET&s=EMD_EPD2D_PTE_NUS_DPG&f=W) and the [Gasoline and Diesel Fuel Update](https://www.eia.gov/petroleum/gasdiesel/) ($6.529 the week of Sep 21, 2026, the series high since March 1994; $6.199 the week of Oct 5; the 2022 high was $5.810).

# Issue 2, in Plain Numbers · The Well · DNSC

> What Lakota's Issue 2 school bond means for your property tax bill if it passes or fails, from the public record.

Issue 2, in Plain Numbers · The Lakota school bond, from the public record

Tax year 2025 rates · Lakota Local School District · Tax district M56, West Chester Township · Revised Oct 23, 2026

## What Issue 2 means for your tax bill

Issue 2 is the Lakota Local School District bond on the November 3, 2026 ballot in Butler County, Ohio. Type in your home to see what it means for your tax bill, with every number cited to the public record.

**Why this exists**

The official figures are spread across several documents: millage, abstracts, roll-offs, a plan in one PDF and a ballot line in another. This tool brings them into one place, each traced to its public source, as an example of a new kind of helpful tool for citizens.

A text field: Appraised value, starting at $350,000.

A slider sets Appraised value from 120000 to 800000, starting at 350000.

On your tax bill and the county's [property search](https://propertysearch.bcohio.gov/).

Taxable value (35%)

Or try a real Lakota home:

**More both comparisons, in full**

**School-bond levies on this home, per year**

| Levy | Today (2026) | 2029 if it passes | 2029 if it fails |
|---|---|---|---|
| School-bond tax per year |  |  |  |

The 2029 columns are estimates.

**More how the rate works, credits, sources**

**How the rate works.** A bond is a fixed amount of debt. Each year the county sets the millage so it collects only that year's payment, spread across every property in the district. When home values rise, the rate goes down, so the district collects the same dollars and no more. For a home whose value rises along with the district's, the bill stays about the same over the life of the bond; a home that rises faster than average pays a little more, and one that rises slower pays a little less. If values fell, the rate would rise to cover the same payment. The 2.20 mills on the ballot is the estimated average over 37 years.[*]

Your actual bill is a bit lower after state credits; the old bonds get them, and Issue 2 would not. None of this includes the possible operating levy below, which is not on this ballot.

*** About the rate.** Ohio law has the county auditor estimate an *average* rate over the life of the bonds, assuming equal yearly principal and flat property values (Ohio Revised Code 133.18 and 5705.218). Each year the county levies what that year's payment needs, so a given year can come in a little above or below 2.20 mills. What is fixed is the amount borrowed, $223,483,492.

Older debt: the district says about 2.2 of today’s 2.28 bond mills roll off after 2028. Smaller older series run through 2035, about $2 million a year. Whether they are paid from the voted bond levy or the permanent-improvement fund is not yet confirmed (see "Unknown" in the fine print). If the levy pays them, up to about a third of a mill could stay on the bill either way; this table leaves that line out.[7]

Source: Issue 2 ballot language and board resolution (June 9, 2026); Ohio DTE 27 tax rate abstract, tax year 2025; Lakota audited debt schedule, FY2025. Figures as of Oct 2, 2026.[6][1][2]

### How an Ohio school district is paid for

Lakota's schools run mostly on local property tax. Under Ohio law a voted operating levy collects about the same dollars as homes gain value, so districts go back to voters every few years.[13][44][17]

#### Where Lakota's money comes from

Lakota levies no school income tax.[14] State aid follows a formula that weighs each district's property wealth and its residents' income.[47]

Of each dollar Lakota took in during fiscal 2024, about 65 cents came from local sources, most of it property tax, and about 29 cents from the state.[13]

57.4¢ · 28.8¢

- Local property tax **57.4¢**
- Other local money **7.3¢**
- State **28.8¢**
- Federal **6.6¢**

US Census count. The district's prospectus counts the state's credits on homeowners' bills as local money: 75 cents local for fiscal 2025.[15]

#### A voted levy raises about the same dollars every year

Under House Bill 920 (1976), the state lowers each voted operating levy's effective rate as values rise, so it collects about what it did the year before from the same homes.[43][44][17] After Lakota's 2023 value update raised taxable values 32.9 percent, its effective operating rate on homes fell from 30.28 mills to 23.29.[14][16]

Districts at a 20-mill floor (477 of Ohio's 611 in 2024) get growth again; Lakota is above it.[44][10]

In the district's forecast, with no new levy, spending runs ahead of revenue every year from fiscal 2025 and cash falls below zero in 2030.[4][14]

[Chart: Line chart of Lakota's general fund, fiscal 2024 to 2031, from the district's August 2026 forecast with no new levies. Revenue: $210.0 million in 2024, $221.0 million in 2026, $240.4 million forecast for 2031. Spending: $205.2 million in 2024, $225.8 million in 2026, $250.9 million forecast for 2031. Spending is above revenue every year from 2025.]

Operating money

Teachers, buses and daily costs. Lakota's last operating levy passed in November 2013, by 288 votes.[44][21]

Building money, like Issue 2

Issue 2 borrows $223,483,492 over up to 37 years, for the buildings in the plan and their debt only. Its rate resets each year to cover that year's payment.[6][44]

#### Lakota's bond and levy votes, 1994 to 2026

The 2013 operating levy was forecast to last five years; the district says it "is still funding the District in 2026, 13 years later."[59] Its forecast assumes a 3.6-mill operating levy from 2029, on no ballot yet.[4] Statewide, 24 of 66 school levies passed in May 2026.[61]

Filled circles passed and open circles failed: Lakota's passes in 2005 and 2013 each came after three failed tries.[21][12][19]

2. **2000** Bond, levy
3. **2004-05** Three tries
4. **2005** Bond, levy
5. **2010-11** Three levy tries
6. **2013** Levy
7. **2025** Issue 10
8. **2026** Issue 2, on the ballot

### The state's share of Lakota's revenue: 38 percent in 2003, 29 percent in 2024

Per student, in 2025 dollars, state revenue fell 28 percent from fiscal 2005 to 2024 while local revenue rose 4 percent.[13]

The state's share (gold) peaked at 38.3 percent in 2003 and was 28.8 percent in 2024; local sources (green) stayed between 56 and 68 percent in every year.[13]

[Chart: Line chart of Lakota revenue shares by source, fiscal 1992 to 2024, US Census count. Local sources stay between about 56 and 68 percent and are 64.7 percent in 2024. The state share is 35.1 percent in 1992, peaks at 38.3 percent in 2003, is 37.3 percent in 2011 and 28.8 percent in 2024. Federal is 1 to 9 percent.]

**More how the shares are counted, what changed along the way, per-pupil dollars**

**How we count.** These shares come from the US Census Bureau, which counts the state's rollback and homestead payments (the state's share of many homeowners' school taxes) as state money. The state's own district report does the same and puts Lakota's state share at 27.9 percent for fiscal 2025.[16] The district's 2026 Financial Prospectus counts that money as local and shows 75 percent local, 21 percent state and 4 percent federal for fiscal 2025.[15] This section uses the Census count throughout. Each year's shares are scaled to add to 100; federal shares in 2021 to 2023 include one-time pandemic aid.

##### What changed along the way

**1997, DeRolph I.** The Ohio Supreme Court rules that the state's school funding system violates the constitution's "thorough and efficient" clause. Lakota's state share rose from 33.9 percent in fiscal 2001 to 38.3 percent in 2003.[18][13]

**2013, House Bill 59.** The state's rollback (10 percent, plus 2.5 percent on owner-occupied homes) ends for levies passed on or after Nov. 5, 2013. Lakota's 2013 levy passed that day, so homeowners pay its full cost.[17]

**2021, the guarantee.** The state's new formula (House Bill 110) calculates less aid for Lakota than it received in fiscal 2021, so a guarantee holds it at that level. In the district's fiscal 2027 forecast, the guarantee is $24.4 million on top of $23.3 million in formula aid. The forecast says, "We are considered a guarantee district and do not anticipate increases in state aid."[14][17]

**2023, the value update.** Property values rise 32.9 percent. Under House Bill 920, Lakota's effective residential operating rate falls from 30.28 to 23.29 mills.[14][16]

**2011 to 2024.** The state's share was 37.3 percent in fiscal 2011 and fell in 11 of the next 13 years.[13]

**Against the state average.** The state's own report puts Lakota's fiscal 2025 state share at 27.9 percent; the average Ohio district's was 37.0 percent.[16][37]

**Revenue per pupil, all funds**

| Measure | FY2005 | FY2024 | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| State, as reported | $3,260 | $3,755 | +15% |
| Local, as reported | $5,067 | $8,448 | +67% |
| State, in 2025 dollars | $5,376 | $3,854 | −28% |
| Local, in 2025 dollars | $8,355 | $8,671 | +4% |

Consumer prices rose about 61 percent from 2005 to 2024 (CPI-U, annual average). The 2025-dollar figures use the same index. The changes are our arithmetic on the Census figures.[13]

Source: US Census Bureau, Annual Survey of School System Finances, all funds, fiscal 1992 to 2024 (the Census has not yet published 2025); Ohio Department of Education and Workforce, District Profile Reports; Lakota FY27 forecast assumptions. Policy dates from the Ohio Legislative Service Commission and the Ohio Supreme Court.[13][16][14][17][18]

### Who pays for Ohio's schools: the record as of October 23, 2026

- **Property owners**: Property tax paid 57.4 percent of Lakota's revenue in fiscal 2024, and homeowners pay the full amount of levies passed since November 5, 2013, with no state rollback.[13][17]
- **Income-tax payers**: Lakota has none, and its board voted down an earned-income-tax option in May 2026; Fairfield City Schools, also in Butler County, asks for one on November 3.[14][6][5]
- **The state**: The 2025 budget finishes the formula on 2022 cost figures, with aid to traditional districts up 0.4 percent in fiscal 2026 and 1.3 percent in 2027;[47] Republican House members' releases call it "nearly $700 million more for public education over the biennium."[57]
- **The courts**: The Ohio Supreme Court found the system unconstitutional in 1997, 2000 and 2002, naming overreliance on local property tax in 2000, and in 2003 left the remedy to the General Assembly.[18][46]

Still open in the record: how the cost of Ohio's schools is shared among property owners, income-tax payers and the state from here.

### More from the record

**What the $300.6 million plan would build $223.5 million local, about $77 million from the state.**

Local taxpayers would pay $223.5 million and the state about $77 million. Grades 6 to 12 move into 4 campuses, and 21 buildings become 18.

The four campus projects come to about $230 million of the $300.6 million.[8]

The plan costs $300.6 million. The state would pay 33 percent of the $233.8 million co-funded work (about $77 million in the April plan; $76.7 million in the state's July approval).

##### What the district says it would do

**All students.** Fewer grade bands: preschool, K to 5, 6 to 8, 9 to 12, and more time in each building.

**Elementary.** Less crowding and smaller classes as sixth graders move to middle schools; art, music and gym all year.

**Middle and high school.** More electives, starting in sixth grade; freshmen on the main high school campus.

**Operations.** Three fewer buildings to run; fewer traveling teachers; bus routes that could support a return of K to 12 busing.

Source: Lakota Local Schools mailer, "Know the Facts: Master Facilities Plan and Nov. 3 Bond Issue," October 2026. These are the district's projections.

Source: Lakota board presentation "The Plan," April 13, 2026; Ohio Facilities Construction Commission conditional approval, July 28, 2026.[8]

The school line is the widest part of the bill: 26.60 of about 47.13 effective mills.[3]

**A 3.6-mill operating levy in the district's forecast A planning placeholder from 2029, on no ballot.**

The board approved the five-year forecast on Aug. 24, 2026. The levy itself is not approved and not filed, and its size and timing could change. The treasurer's notes say savings from the facilities plan could reduce or remove the need for it. It is here so a voter can see the district's whole forecast alongside this year's ballot.

Without new money, the forecast's general-fund cash falls each year and goes below zero in fiscal 2030.[4]

Source: Lakota Five-Year Forecast and its notes (including the FY2025 transfers), approved by the board Aug 24, 2026. FY2027 on are projections.[4]

##### What the forecast assumes

**The levy.** 3.6 mills, collected from 2029 in the Aug. 24 forecast. Not filed and on no ballot as of Oct. 7, 2026.

**What it would raise.** $11.3 million in FY2029, $21.8 million in FY2030.

Enrollment rose to a peak of 18,473 in 2009-10 and was 17,564 in 2023-24; the dashed projection counts students a little differently.[19][9]

By the district's count in its audited reports, enrollment rose from 10,205 in 1991-92 to a peak of 18,473 in 2009-10. It fell to 15,991 in 2014-15 and was 17,564 in 2023-24.[19]

A March 2026 projection by FutureThink, done at the state's request, shows 16,754 students in 2033-34 and 16,555 by 2035-36. It counts students a little differently, leaving out regular preschool and full-time career-tech students. The same firm's July 2024 projection showed 19,074 for 2033-34.[9][20]

The district's FAQ says: "According to the Ohio Facilities Construction Commission's (OFCC) guidelines, Lakota is overcapacity by more than 700 students, when comparing our enrollment to the size of our schools."[7]

Effective residential mills are the operating rate on homes and farms after House Bill 920 reductions, tax year 2024. Property value is assessed value as the state reports it. The Ohio average is the average district. Lakota was rated 4.5 stars in 2024-25, one of four districts here at 4.5 with Dublin, Sycamore and Forest Hills; Olentangy and Mason were rated 5. The 2025-26 report card again rates Lakota 4.5.[37][38]

##### The bond record, 2015 to 2026

**Building bonds.** 9 of the 14 peers in the ballot review put a building bond on the ballot since 2015, and all 9 passed at least one; 14 of their 20 bond questions passed. Mason, Fairfield, Hamilton City, Princeton and Forest Hills had no bond vote in that time. West Clermont was not part of the ballot review.[40]

**Olentangy failed, then passed.** A $350 million bond with two levies got 36.6 percent in March 2024. Twenty months later, a bond-only $235 million, 33 percent smaller, passed with 56.2 percent.[40]

**Pickerington failed twice, then passed.** A $95 million bond got 47.0 percent in November 2020 and 39.1 percent in May 2021. An $89.9 million bond passed in November 2022 with 57.6 percent.[40]

**Kings failed twice, then passed.** A junior high bond got 49.0 percent in November 2019 and 48.6 percent in April 2020. A $142 million high school bond passed in March 2024 with 52.7 percent.[40]

**Lakota's Issue 10.** Its 39.2 percent in November 2025 is among the three weakest building-bond results in this set, with Olentangy's 36.6 percent and Pickerington's 39.1 percent. Both of those districts later passed a bond.[12][40]

**On the same ballot.** South-Western City asks voters on Nov 3, 2026 for a $220 million bond at 2.26 mills over 38 years.[41]

**What followed failures.** Most documented cuts after a failure followed failed operating levies or income taxes: Fairfield cut busing to the state minimum after March 2024, Princeton froze hiring and cut 40 positions over two years after November 2024, and Pickerington made $3.28 million a year in first-phase cuts after May 2026. Westerville (33 positions) and Olentangy (redistricting, modular classrooms, larger classes and new fees) made cuts after questions that paired a bond with operating money. After the bond-only failures in Kings and Pickerington from 2019 to 2021, we found no documented cuts.[42]

**The bond chart.** Each bar is a bond's face amount divided by the district's October 2025 headcount (17,013 for Lakota): $223.5 million for Issue 2 and $506.4 million for Issue 10. Older bonds use today's enrollment and are not adjusted for inflation, so they look smaller than they were. Sycamore's bar uses its $127.5 million program cost, because the bond's face amount was not confirmed. South-Western's 2018 bar is its local share; the state added about the same. The median of the 13 passed peer bonds with a known face amount is about $8,270 per student.[39][40][6][7]

##### Cautions

**Student counts differ.** The state counts 16,736 Lakota students for fiscal 2025, and the table's per-pupil figures use the state's count for every district. The district's own counts run higher: 17,564 in 2023-24 in its audited report and 17,249 in 2025-26 in the FutureThink study.[37][19][9]

**Economic disadvantage is left out.** Pickerington and Hamilton City report nearly every student as economically disadvantaged (99.7 and 100 percent), which reflects how students were counted, so that measure does not compare across these districts.[37]

**Forest Hills is incomplete.** Its ballot record for 2015 to 2018 and late 2023 to 2026 could not be fully checked, and its 2014 bond amount was not found.[40]

**State share.** The state's report counts rollback and homestead payments as state money; the district's prospectus counts them as local (see "How we count," above).[37][15]

**Size.** Five of the neighbors (Sycamore, Kings, Princeton, Forest Hills and West Clermont) enroll under half as many students as Lakota.[37]

Source: Ohio Department of Education and Workforce, FY2025 District Profile Report and October 2025 enrollment headcount; Ohio School Report Cards, 2024-25 and 2025-26; county boards of elections results and notices, 2015 to 2026; news reports on cuts, as listed in the sources.[37][38][39][40][41][42]

**Band and the arts under the plan Band from grade 6, the district says.**

Sixth grade would move to the middle schools, where the district says electives would begin.[7]

**Today and under the plan, in the district's words**

| Program | Today | Under the plan |
|---|---|---|
| Band | Starts in grade 7 | "Access to electives, including band, beginning in sixth grade" |
| Choir | Starts in junior high (grades 7 and 8) | Not stated |
| Theater | "Beginning as early as junior high" | Not stated |
| Elementary art | "A weekly hands-on experience in producing art" | "Consistent, year-round specials (e.g. art, music, gym)" in K-5 |
| Sixth grade | In elementary schools (grades 3 to 6) | In middle schools (grades 6 to 8) |

**Houston, a randomized study Bowen and Kisida, 2019 · Fewer discipline infractions and better writing; no significant effect on math, reading, science or attendance.**

42 schools chosen by lottery; 10,548 students in grades 3 to 8; school years 2015-16 and 2016-17.[23]

**Found:** 3.6 percentage points fewer students with discipline infractions; writing scores up 0.13 standard deviations; compassion up 0.08. No significant effect on math, reading, science or attendance.

**Limits:** The program added arts partnerships (performances, field trips, artist residencies) at about $14.67 per student a year, separate from school band or art classes. Principals volunteered, Houston is arts-rich, and the results cover two years only.

**OECD review of the research Winner, Goldstein and Vincent-Lancrin, 2013 · Classroom drama strengthens verbal skills; experiments do not yet show arts classes raising academic results.**

Studies in 11 languages.[24]

**Found:** Classroom drama strengthens verbal skills. Experimental studies of arts classes "do not (yet) show a significant causal impact" on academic results, and there is "no evidence that music education has any causal impact on mathematics scores." Its conclusion: "the main justification for arts education is clearly the acquisition of artistic habits of mind."

**Limits:** Written before the Houston study. Later reviews dispute its finding on music and IQ.

**What Ohio law requires Ohio Revised Code 3313.60 and 3313.603 · Every district's curriculum must include "the fine arts, including music."**

Ohio Revised Code 3313.60 and 3313.603.[25]

**Found:** Every district's curriculum must include "the fine arts, including music." Most students need two semesters of fine arts, taken in grades 7 to 12, to graduate.

**Limits:** We found no state minimum for elementary art or music time, and no required ratio of arts teachers since 2015. That search was not a full legal review.

Band starts in grade 7 today. Under the plan, sixth grade moves to the middle schools, and the district says electives, including band, would begin in grade 6.[22][7]

Choir and theater start in junior high, and elementary art is weekly, per the district's pages.[22] The district says K-5 students would get "consistent, year-round specials." Its FAQ also says that if the bond passes, "all programs will be reviewed," including K-5 specials.[7]

Source: Lakota Arts and Activities, K-6 Specials and Kindergarten pages; Lakota FAQ, updated Sept 25, 2026; the studies and statutes named on each card.[22][7][23][24][25]

**Two paths, in time What happens next if Issue 2 passes or fails.**

A choice (Show a path step by step): If Issue 2 passes, If Issue 2 fails.

##### If Issue 2 passes

1. **Nov 3, 2026 · Voters decide Issue 2.** Voters decide Issue 2: $223,483,492 in bonds over up to 37 years, an estimated average of 2.20 mills.[6]
2. **About Feb 1, 2027 · The bonds are dated.** The bonds are dated, at an estimated 5.00 percent average interest rate in the board's resolution.[6]
3. **After the vote, before construction · A new traffic study.** A new traffic study for entrances, exits and traffic flow. "A new traffic study will need to be done to determine the final options for traffic flow, including entrance/exit locations." The FAQ adds: "Safety and traffic flow will be reviewed again prior to construction beginning."[7]
4. **Next · Designs and construction begin.** Designs and construction begin. "We would begin construction," the superintendent says. [06:45][36]
5. After 2028 About 2.2 mills of older bonds roll off.[7]
6. **2029 · Collection of the new 2.2 mills begins.** Collection of the new 2.2 mills begins. The superintendent calls it "an anticipated no new tax increase." [13:38][36] The calculator above shows the cost against today and against a failed vote.
7. **Start of the 2029-30 school year · Students move into the new buildings and grade bands.** Students move into the new and renovated buildings and the new grade bands: preschool, K to 5, 6 to 8 and 9 to 12. [06:50][36][7]
8. **After occupancy · Four buildings are demolished.** Adena, Ridge, Central/Creekside and West Freshman are demolished. [07:03][36]
9. **2029-30 on, K to 5 · Smaller classes and year-round specials, per the superintendent.** Class sizes, "instead of sitting at 27 plus is going to look more like 23 or 24," and specials in "year round rotations" in place of "short stints in art and music and P.E.," per the superintendent. [04:29, 04:42][36]
10. **2029-30 on, grades 6 to 8 · Sixth graders move to middle school.** Sixth graders move to middle school with "earlier access to electives." [05:03] The FAQ says electives, "including band," begin in sixth grade.[36][7]
11. **After the move · Fewer traveling teachers and three fewer buildings.** "Fewer traveling teachers," the superintendent says, [08:33] and three fewer buildings to maintain, per the FAQ.[36][7]

##### If Issue 2 fails

1. Nov 3, 2026 Issue 2 does not pass.
2. **After the vote · The grade bands cannot change, the FAQ says.** "If the bond issue is not approved, we cannot shift the grade-band configuration, which is necessary to address overcrowding and large class sizes," the FAQ says.[7]
3. **After the vote · The district's traffic study waits on the vote.** The district's traffic study waits on the vote. The FAQ says the study "is pending the outcome of the Nov. 3 vote by the community due to its cost."[7]
4. **Today, per the district · Overcrowding stays as the district describes it.** Overcrowding stays as the district describes it: "overcapacity by more than 700 students," and "many K-5 classrooms have 27 or more students, with some classes exceeding 30."[7]
5. **Next, what gets cut · The district's own list: specials, electives, and all-day kindergarten moving to tuition.** "Other options will need to be considered, including all-day kindergarten." The FAQ adds: "there are other options that would be considered before eliminating all-day kindergarten because of its educational impact. These options include specials, electives and a tuition-based all-day kindergarten."[7] Today Lakota offers all-day kindergarten to all families, with a half-day morning option.[22]
6. After 2028 The older bonds' 2.2 mills still roll off, and the school-bond line on the bill goes to $0.[7]
7. **Later ballots · Two more tries before the state's $77 million goes elsewhere.** "Lakota will have two additional attempts at passing a bond issue. If a bond issue is not approved by voters after three attempts, the OFCC will apply the $77 million to another district's facilities plan," the FAQ says. The superintendent calls it "three strikes and you're out." [11:27][7][36]

**Either way.** The forecast's assumed 3.6-mill operating levy, collected from 2029, applies whether Issue 2 passes or fails.[4]

Source: Lakota Master Facilities Plan FAQ, updated Sept 25, 2026; district post "The Big Picture," Sept 25, 2026; Resolution to Proceed, June 9, 2026; "2026 Master Facilities Plan and November Bond Information," district video, Oct 6, 2026, with minute marks from its captions; Five-Year Forecast, Aug 24, 2026. These are the district's statements and plans.[7][6][36][4]

**The laws and rulings behind the levy cycle, 1976 to 2026 House Bill 920, DeRolph, the formula, 2025 changes.**

1. **1976 · House Bill 920 A voted operating levy raises about the same dollars every year When home values rise, its effective rate falls.** Each year the state sets a reduction factor for each voted operating and permanent improvement levy so that it collects about what it collected the year before from property already on the tax list. The Legislative Service Commission's summary: "each year when property values increase, tax collections are adjusted downward so that taxing districts receive the same amount of revenue they received in the previous year."[43][44] New money for a district comes from new construction, unvoted (inside) millage, which is not reduced, and new levies.[44][17] There is a floor. A district's operating rate cannot be reduced below 20 mills; at the floor, the bill follows values up. In 2024, 477 of Ohio's 611 city, local and exempted village districts were at the floor.[44] Lakota's operating levies are above it.[10] Bond levies, like Issue 2, are outside the reduction factor. Their rate is set each year to collect that year's debt payment.[44][6]
2. **1997 to 2003 · DeRolph v. State The Ohio Supreme Court ruled three times that school funding was unconstitutional In 2003 it ended the case and left the fix to the legislature.** **March 24, 1997, DeRolph I, 4 to 3.** The system violated the constitution's call for "a thorough and efficient system of common schools."[18][46] **May 1998.** A one-cent sales tax for schools went to voters and lost, 79.91 to 20.09 percent.[46] **May 11, 2000, DeRolph II.** Still unconstitutional. Among seven items to fix, the court listed overreliance on local property tax and "phantom revenue," which includes "property tax revenue credited to a school district when its tax base increases, but which is never actually received by the district due to ... tax-reduction factors."[18][46] **September 2001, DeRolph III.** The Court found most of the new system complied and said it would be constitutional once the state made further changes, including full funding of parity aid by July 1, 2003.[18][46] **December 11, 2002, DeRolph IV.** The Court vacated that order and held that "the current school funding system is unconstitutional."[18][46] **May 16, 2003.** The court ended the litigation: "The duty now lies with the General Assembly to remedy an educational system that has been found by the majority in DeRolph IV to still be unconstitutional." The Legislative Service Commission noted in August 2024 that "no new case has been filed."[46]
3. **2020 to 2025 · federal pandemic relief The federal pandemic money for schools is spent Lakota's last ESSER dollars show up in its fiscal 2024 audit.** Ohio's schools received $7.14 billion in federal pandemic relief. Most of it came in three rounds of ESSER, the Elementary and Secondary School Emergency Relief fund: $489.2 million, $1.99 billion and an estimated $4.47 billion. The third round was available through September 30, 2024.[48] Beside Lakota, two nearby districts in this series for comparison, both with operating levies on recent ballots: Troy City in Miami County and Talawanda in Butler County.[52][53] **ESSER spent, by fiscal year, in each district's state audit[49][50][51]** | Year | Lakota | Troy City | Talawanda | |---|---|---|---| | 2020 | $597,959 | none | none | | 2021 | $2,232,014 | $408,456 | $269,183 | | 2022 | $6,047,385 | $1,854,673 | $1,008,095 | | 2023 | $6,418,228 | $2,168,028 | $1,322,173 | | 2024 | $3,471,651 | $1,929,206 | $1,445,175 | | 2025 | none | $1,306,035 | $116,007 | | Total | $18,767,237 | $7,666,398 | $4,160,633 | Fiscal years end June 30. The figures are the audits' ESSER lines (federal listings 84.425D and 84.425U); lines for homeless students are left out. Bars share one scale, Lakota's 2023 at full width. Troy's fiscal 2024 audit totals $1,940,706 in the fund, $11,500 of it for homeless students.[49][50][51] **Troy City Schools.** Its 5.8-mill operating renewal, first passed in 1996 and renewed every five years since, failed in May 2026. It is on the November 3, 2026 ballot again.[52] **Talawanda.** A 5.7-mill operating levy failed on November 8, 2022, with 35.17 percent for. The district has no issue on the November 2026 ballot.[53] **Lakota.** Its fiscal 2025 audit lists no ESSER spending.[49]
4. **2021 to 2025 · House Bills 110 and 96 A new state formula was built, then finished on 2022 costs Statewide, aid to traditional districts rises 0.4 percent in fiscal 2026 and 1.3 percent in 2027.** House Bill 110 (2021) prices a base cost per student from staffing and salary inputs, then splits it between the state and the district by local property wealth and income. It was phased in over six years.[47][17] The 2025 budget, House Bill 96, completes the phase-in in fiscal 2026 and 2027 "while maintaining FY 2022 base cost inputs," and extends two guarantees that keep a district from falling below its 2020 or 2021 aid.[47] State foundation aid for traditional districts is estimated at $8.15 billion in fiscal 2026 and $8.26 billion in fiscal 2027, increases of 0.4 and 1.3 percent. Aid to community and STEM schools rises 4.8 and 5.0 percent.[47] Republican House members' releases on the final budget put it at "nearly $700 million more for public education over the biennium than they received in FY25."[57] State scholarship (voucher) spending was $394.2 million in fiscal 2020 and $1.09 billion in fiscal 2025; House Bill 33 (2023) opened EdChoice Expansion to families of all incomes.[60] Lakota is on the guarantee. Its fiscal 2027 forecast carries $24.4 million in guarantee aid on top of $23.3 million from the formula.[14]
5. **2025 · the veto override The legislature changed which levies districts may ask for Replacement and substitute levies end; new emergency levies are only for districts in fiscal distress.** The governor signed the budget, House Bill 96, on June 30, 2025, with 67 line-item vetoes. The House overrode item 66 on July 21, 2025, 61 to 28, and the Senate on October 1, 2025, 21 to 11.[55][54][56][11] The House Republican release on the Senate vote said the provision "ensures taxpayers have more control over their property tax bills." The House Democratic leader's release on July 21 called the override "not real property tax relief."[62] Item 66 ends new replacement levies, renewals with an increase, and new emergency and substitute levies (both raise a fixed dollar sum). It also bars a new operating levy when a district's prior-year carryover exceeds 100 percent of its expenses.[58][43] Under the statute as amended since (House Bill 129, in effect March 20, 2026), a new emergency levy is open only to a district in fiscal caution, watch or emergency (the state's three levels of financial distress) or after a declared disaster, and an emergency or substitute levy approved before January 1, 2026 can be renewed only at the same or a smaller sum, up to five years at a time.[55][43][63] On December 19, 2025, the governor signed five more property tax bills, in effect March 20, 2026. House Bill 186 caps growth at inflation for districts at the 20-mill floor; House Bill 335 caps growth in unvoted millage.[56][11] Other vetoed items stay open to an override vote through December 31, 2026. Two of them bear on school levies: county budget commission power to cut voted levies (item 55), and a rule letting those commissions cut a district's levies when its carryover tops 40 percent of a year's spending (item 63).[55][54] Lakota's current carryover percentage: Unknown In May 2026, 24 of 66 Ohio school levies passed. As of September 18, the Secretary of State's list carried 131 school tax issues for November 3, 68 for new money, by one outside count; a regional station counted "more than 130 education issues" on October 7.[61]

Sources: Ohio Revised Code 319.301 and 5705.194; Ohio Legislative Service Commission briefs on millage floors (Sept. 19, 2025) and DeRolph (Aug. 12, 2024) and its House Bill 96 education budget analysis (Sept. 2025); Butler County Auditor; Ohio Department of Education relief summary (April 29, 2021); Ohio Auditor of State single audits for Lakota, Troy City and Talawanda; the Ohio House Journal for July 21, 2025; House member releases and candidates' own pages, each dated where it carries a date. Figures as of October 21, 2026.[43][44][46][47][10][48][49][54][58]

**Fine print: sources, timeline and method**

**The public records behind these numbers**

Verified **Ohio Division of Tax Equalization, DTE 27 Abstract of Tax Rates, tax year 2025, Butler County, Lakota LSD.** Two bond levies are on the books:[1]

| Rate | Purpose | Voted | Term | Levy authorized through |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1.000 | Bond ($44,571,000) | Nov 7, 2000 | 26 yrs | tax year 2025 (collected 2026) |
| 1.280 | Bond ($84,300,000) | Nov 8, 2005 | 28 yrs | tax year 2032 |
| **2.280** | **total bond mills today** |  |  |  |

The "authorized through" year is how long the levy *may* run, not when the debt is paid. The payoff date is set by the bonds themselves, and those were refunded. The district's Sept 25, 2026 post says the same: four series totaling $34.9 million, an average 2.28 mills needed 2026 to 2028, the 2005 series paid off in 2026, the 2020 series in 2027, the 2020A series in 2028.[7]

Verified **Ohio Auditor of State, Lakota LSD audited financial statements, FY2023, debt note.** The 2005-dated series (the 2006 Refunding) matures December 1, 2026. The 2020 Refunding matures December 1, 2027. The 2013 refunding of the 2005 bonds matures December 1, 2029. The only series maturing in 2034 is the 2014 school improvement bonds.[2] Updated by the **FY2025 audit** (opinion dated Dec 26, 2025): bonds outstanding $61.58M principal at June 30, 2025; the 2006 Refunding ($9.66M) matures Dec 1, 2026; the 2020 Refunding ($13.9M) Dec 1, 2027; the 2020A and 2020B refundings ($30.9M) carry no printed maturity; a 2016 refunding runs to Dec 1, 2033. Debt service by fiscal year: FY2026 $14.44M, FY2027 $14.20M, FY2028 $14.22M, FY2029 $12.42M (the last big maturity, paid from taxes collected in 2028), FY2030 $2.09M, then about $2.0M a year through FY2035. The audit's note: bonds are paid "from the debt service and permanent improvement funds." In FY2025 the debt-service fund paid $9.47M and the permanent-improvement fund $1.81M.[2]

Unknown Whether the smaller series after 2028 are paid from the voted bond levy or from the 2-mill permanent-improvement fund. That decides whether a residual of up to about a third of a mill stays on the bill in 2029 to 2035 either way. A public-records request for the debt-service schedule by series and by fund settles it.

Verified **The county's own Levy Calculator, run on a West Chester home appraised at $322,330 (taxable $112,820), Sept 29 and again Oct 2, 2026.** It shows the Lakota bond as **Current Tax $0.00, Additional Tax $248.20**. The same parcel's Current Tax Distribution tab shows the two existing Lakota bonds at 2.28 mills, **$257.21** a year. The calculator shows only the new levy; the current bond tax is on the separate distribution tab.[3]

Verified **An operating levy is in the district's own five-year forecast**, approved by the board Feb 23, 2026 and again Aug 24, 2026: a new **3.6-mill** operating levy assumed to pass in 2028 and collect from 2029 ($11.3M in FY2029, $21.8M in FY2030). It is on no ballot. It would apply whether Issue 2 passes or fails.[4]

Verified **Issue 2 as certified by the Butler County Board of Elections and the board's June 9, 2026 resolution (5 to 0):** a bond issue of $223,483,492 over 37 years, estimated average 2.20 mills, about $77 per $100,000 of market value on a certified taxable value of $5,338,361,890, bonds dated about Feb 1, 2027 at an estimated net average interest rate of 5.00%, first collection 2029.[5][6] **Total repayment, estimated:** at the resolution's 5% estimate and level payments over 37 years, total repayment would be roughly $495 million, about $13.4 million a year, of which about $271 million is interest. That is an arithmetic estimate from the resolution's own figures, not a district number; the real schedule depends on the rates when the bonds sell.[6]

Verified **One mill in Lakota is about $5.34 million** on the taxable value the county auditor certified for the resolution ($5,338,361,890).[6] The 2026 reappraisal raised values countywide by a median of 19 percent (auditor's FAQ, June 30, 2026);[10] the district's August forecast assumes 9 percent for homes.[4] Because a bond levy raises a fixed dollar amount, higher values mean fewer mills, not more dollars.

Verified **The ballot question, as the board's June 9, 2026 resolution sets it:** "Shall bonds be issued by the Lakota Local School District... in the principal amount of $223,483,492, to be repaid annually over a maximum period of 37 years, and an annual levy of property taxes be made outside the ten-mill limitation, estimated by the county auditor to average over the repayment period of the bond issue 2.20 mills for each $1 of taxable value, which amounts to $77 for each $100,000 of the county auditor's market value, commencing in 2028, first due in calendar year 2029..."[6]

Verified **The votes (board roll calls).** May 20, 2026, resolution of necessity: passed 4 to 1. The same night an earned-income-tax alternative failed 2 to 3. June 9, 2026, resolution to proceed: passed 5 to 0.[6]

Verified **What the money builds (board deck, April 13, 2026, "The Plan").** Plains Junior addition and renovation $58.7M; East Freshman addition and renovation $55.3M; East High School campus $57.6M; West High School campus $58.3M; demolition of Ridge, Adena and Creekside/West Freshman about $3.8M; locally funded items $51.5M; permanent improvements $15.3M. Total $300.6M ($300,627,663); state share 33 percent of the $233.8M co-funded work, about $77.1M; local share $223,483,492. Grades K to 5 stay in 13 elementaries; 6 to 8 at East Freshman and Plains; 9 to 12 at East and West. Twenty-one buildings become eighteen. The state's Facilities Construction Commission gave conditional approval July 28, 2026 (Classroom Facilities Assistance Program, Segment One): state share $76,681,895, and the board must accept by Nov 25, 2026.[8]

Verified **Enrollment (FutureThink study, done at the state's request, March 11, 2026):** 17,249 students in all in 2025 to 26. On the study's projection basis (16,913, which leaves out regular preschool and full-time JVS students), enrollment peaks near 17,116 in 2029 to 30 and ends 358 lower by 2035 to 36. The district's March 26, 2026 post says the state's 2024 study had forecast about 2,000 more students over ten years; its FAQ says buildings are over capacity by more than 700 today.[9][7]

Verified **The credits are changing under state law.** The 10 percent non-business and 2.5 percent owner-occupancy credits apply only to levies approved before late 2013; the state abstract marks the 2000 and 2005 bonds as qualifying, and a new bond would not.[1][10] House Bill 186 raises the owner-occupancy credit (to as much as 15.38 percent) and phases the non-business credit down to zero over four years starting tax year 2026, on qualifying levies only. Its inflation-cap credit is $0 for the Lakota school levies, because the district's operating levies have not reached the 20-mill floor; Lakota homes may still get the Butler Tech (JVSD) portion, estimated at $12.16 per $100,000. House Bill 96's veto override (item 66, completed Oct 1, 2025) ends replacement, emergency and substitute levies for elections on or after Jan 1, 2026. This page shows the bill before credits; your treasurer's bill applies them.[10][11]

**How this bond came to be**

| When | What happened |
|---|---|
| Nov 2000 | Voters approve a $44,571,000 bond, 1.00 mill, 26 years.[1] |
| Nov 2005 | Voters approve an $84,300,000 bond, 1.28 mills, 28 years. Together the two levies are the 2.28 mills on today's bill.[1] |
| 2006 to 2020 | The district refinances those bonds several times at lower rates (refunding series including 2006, 2013, 2016, 2020, 2020A and 2020B), which is why they are paid off years before the levies' authorized end dates.[2] |
| 2024 | A state enrollment study projects about 2,000 more students over ten years. (The district's facilities planning began in 2018.)[7] |
| June 30, 2025 | Board votes 4 to 1 to place a $506,359,503 bond (4.99 mills, $175 per $100,000) and a 0.95-mill permanent-improvement levy ($33 per $100,000) on the November ballot: $208 per $100,000 as written. The district put the net change, after the old bonds end, at 2.66 mills, about $93 per $100,000.[7] |
| Nov 4, 2025 | Voters reject it as Issue 10: 60.8 percent against.[12] |
| Mar 11, 2026 | A new enrollment study (FutureThink) reverses the forecast: 17,249 students now and a projected decline of 358 by 2035 to 36. The district says buildings are over capacity by more than 700 today.[9][7] |
| Apr 13, 2026 | The board sees "The Plan": grades 6 to 12 only, four campuses, $300.6 million total, about $77 million from the state (33 percent of the co-funded work), $223.5 million local, 21 buildings to 18.[7] |
| May 20, 2026 | Resolution of necessity passes 4 to 1. An earned-income-tax alternative fails 2 to 3.[6] |
| June 9, 2026 | Resolution to proceed passes 5 to 0: $223,483,492, 37 years, estimated 2.20 mills, first collection 2029, timed to the old bonds finishing.[6] |
| July 28, 2026 | The Ohio Facilities Construction Commission gives conditional approval; state share $76.7 million; the board must accept by Nov 25, 2026.[8] |
| Aug 17, 2026 | The Board of Elections certifies it as Issue 2.[5] |
| Aug 24, 2026 | The board approves a five-year forecast that again models a 3.6-mill operating levy for 2028, and says the facilities plan's savings could reduce or remove the need for it.[4] |
| Sept 25, 2026 | The district publishes its bond roll-off schedule: four outstanding series totaling $34.9 million, with about 2.2 mills rolling off after 2028.[7] |

**How this is calculated, and how honest it is**

Ohio taxes **35 percent** of a home's appraised value. West Chester Township homes in Lakota are tax district `M56`, about **47 effective mills** on a home; Liberty Township homes in Lakota (`D20`) are about 45 because the township rate is lower, and the school lines are identical. Your bill is that rate on 35 percent of the value you set. One mill is about `$35 per $100,000`.

**Pass or fail:** Issue 2's collection begins in 2029, so it does not change today's bill. The chart compares the 2 outcomes year by year for the value you set. All figures are before credits. Issue 6 is a countywide mental-health renewal at the same rate you pay now.

**Honest about the numbers:** the district rates and ballot figures are the county's TY2025 numbers and the certified ballot; the split across bodies uses each body's effective residential rate from the county. Your treasurer's bill is always the record. Sources: Ohio DTE 27 abstract, tax year 2025; Butler County Auditor 2025 Tax Rates and Levy Calculator; Ohio Auditor of State, Lakota FY2023 and FY2025 audits; Butler County BOE certified Nov 3, 2026 issues; Lakota five-year forecast updates.

# What's in the jar · Cannabis in Ohio · DNSC

> How strong today's cannabis is, what Ohio's law allows, where the money goes, and what the research says, in plain numbers with every source linked.

What's in the jar · Cannabis in Ohio, from the public record

Ohio law as of Mar 20, 2026 · Sales through Sep 19, 2026 · Research through Aug 2026

Ohio · law, money and health

## What's in the jar.

How strong today's cannabis is, what Ohio's law allows, where the money goes, and what the research says. Plain numbers, every source a click away.

[Chart: A line drawing of a jar with a leaf inside]

1 · Then and now

### The weed in today's jar is several times stronger than it was in the 1990s.

Seized flower averaged about 4% THC in 1995. Legal flower now averages about 20%, and concentrates often run 50 to 90%.

Seized flower (DEA samples) · Seized hash oil · Legal market, Washington · Typical concentrates

[Chart: THC potency from 1995 to 2026 with Ohio's legal caps of 35 percent for flower and 70 percent for extracts]

**~4% → ~20%** Average THC in flower, 1995 seized samples to today's legal stores.

**35% cap** Ohio's limit for flower, for medical and adult use alike.

**70% cap** Ohio's limit for extracts since March 20, 2026, down from Issue 2's 90% floor.

**Sources for this part**

The DEA samples are seizures of illegal product, so they understate what legal stores sell. Labels can be off too: in a 2025 Colorado study, only 56.7% of flower products tested within 15% of their labeled THC. No public data on the average THC of products sold in Ohio exists; lab results are reported into the state's tracking system.

- ElSohly et al., [Biological Psychiatry, 2016](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26903403/) (about 4% in 1995 to about 12% in 2014).
- Chandra et al., [Eur Arch Psychiatry Clin Neurosci, 2019](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30671616/) (8.9% in 2008 to 17.1% in 2017; hash oil 6.7% to 55.7%).
- ElSohly et al., [Biol Psychiatry: CNNI, 2021](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33508497/) (14.88% in 2018, 13.88% in 2019).
- Smart, Caulkins, Kilmer et al., [Addiction, 2017](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28556310/) (Washington legal market: flower 20.6%, extracts 68.7%).
- [Int J Drug Policy, 2024](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38043404/) (concentrates 50 to 90% THC).
- [Scientific Reports, 2025](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40592871/) (Colorado label accuracy).
- Ohio Revised Code [3796.06(E)](https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-revised-code/section-3796.06) and the LSC [Final Analysis of S.B. 56](https://www.legislature.ohio.gov/download?key=27450) (35% plant, 70% extract).

How much THC is in that?

A choice (Product): Flower, Dab, Vape cartridge.

A slider sets THC on the label from 1 to 90, starting at 20.

Ohio caps extracts at 70% THC. Stronger products exist in other states and in older stock.

A slider sets Amount from 0.05 to 3.5, starting at 1.

200 mg of THC in it

This counts the THC in the product; how much reaches your body depends on how it's used. Each dot is 10 mg, the most THC Canada allows in a whole package of edibles.

2 · What the law says

### Ohio said yes in 2023, then rewrote the rules in 2026.

Voters passed Issue 2 with 57%. The legislature replaced it with Senate Bill 56, which took effect March 20, 2026 and now governs medical and adult use together.

1. Sep 2016 **Medical marijuana becomes legal** House Bill 523. The first medical sales come in January 2019.
2. Nov 2023 **Issue 2 passes, 57% to 43%** Adults 21 and over can buy, carry and grow at home.
3. Aug 2024 **Adult-use sales begin** At stores licensed for both medical and adult use.
4. Jun 2025 **The budget redirects the tax money** House Bill 96 replaces Issue 2's split. More below.
5. Mar 2026 **Senate Bill 56 takes effect** One law for medical and adult use. Extract cap falls to 70%. Intoxicating hemp moves into dispensaries.
6. Dec 11, 2026 **Federal hemp rule arrives** A new national definition of hemp, delayed one month by Congress.

2.5 oz · **Possession limit** for plant material, plus 15 grams of extract.

6 / 12 · **Home grow:** 6 plants per adult, 12 per home. Going over by any number is now a crime.

0.4 mg · **Hemp limit:** more THC than this per container, and it's legally marijuana, sold only in dispensaries.

400 · **Statewide cap** on dispensaries, at least a mile apart. 231 operate today.

Home · **Smoking and vaping** are allowed only on private residential or farm property.

**The details: what changed with Senate Bill 56**

**Structure.** SB 56 repealed the Issue 2 law (Chapter 3780) and merged both markets into Chapter 3796. Licenses are now dual-use.

**Potency.** 35% THC for plant material and 70% for extracts, for medical and adult use. Issue 2 had told regulators to set limits no lower than 35% and 90%. The state may raise the extract limit by rule. A Division of Cannabis Control guidance sheet dated March 2026 still lists 90% for manufactured products, so confirm with the Division before relying on one number.

**Hemp.** Since March 20, 2026, hemp means no more than 0.3% total THC, including THCA. A finished product with more than 0.4 mg of THC per container, or with cannabinoids made outside the plant (such as delta-8 converted from CBD), is not hemp. A plan to let bars and stores sell hemp drinks was vetoed. A federal court has blocked parts of the ban for ten plaintiff companies; the appeal is pending.

**Other changes.** Marijuana bought out of state is contraband. No new dispensary within a mile of another, or where liquor is sold. Stricter packaging and advertising. A path to expunge past minor possession offenses. Local governments can ban new operators but not home grow, and can't close stores licensed before March 20, 2026.

**Tax.** The 10% rate stayed. An earlier version of SB 56 would have raised it to 15%.

- Ohio Legislative Service Commission, [Final Analysis of S.B. 56](https://www.legislature.ohio.gov/download?key=27450) (corrected Apr 2, 2026) and [bill status](https://www.legislature.ohio.gov/legislation/136/sb56).
- Ohio Revised Code [3796.06](https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-revised-code/section-3796.06), [3796.01](https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-revised-code/section-3796.01), [3796.40](https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-revised-code/section-3796.40).
- Division of Cannabis Control, [Total THC Content Guidance](https://dam.assets.ohio.gov/image/upload/com.ohio.gov/DCC/Total_THC_Content_Guidance.pdf) (03/2026).
- Issue 2 results (57.19% yes): [Wikipedia, citing the Ohio Secretary of State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Ohio_Issue_2).
- Federal hemp: Congressional Research Service, [LSB11381](https://www.everycrsreport.com/files/2025-12-08_LSB11381_8b411fbfb79325154a586ad1fbba21298039afe5.html); the Dec 11, 2026 delay as reported by [Akerman](https://www.akerman.com/en/perspectives/congress-approves-one-month-delay-of-federal-hemp-thc-restrictions.html).
- Hemp litigation: [KMK Law, Aug 2026](https://www.kmklaw.com/cannabis-and-craft-beer/ohio-hemp-ban-stalled-federal-court-sides-with-hemp-industry).

3 · Where the money goes

### By September, adult-use sales had already passed all of 2025.

Ohioans have bought $4.3 billion of legal cannabis since 2019. As adult use grew, the medical program shrank by more than half.

Adult use · Medical · 2026 runs through Sept 19

[Chart: Ohio legal cannabis sales by year, 2019 to 2026, adult use and medical]

**$844M** Adult-use sales in 2026 through Sept 19, versus about $830M in all of 2025.

**10% + sales tax** On adult use. In Butler County the sales tax adds about 6.5%.

**−59%** Active medical patients, from 178,703 in Oct 2023 to 72,943 in Jul 2026.

The 10% tax, under Issue 2

Equity 36% · Host towns 36% · Addiction 25%

Social equity and jobs 36%, host communities 36%, addiction services 25%, administration 3%.

Since June 30, 2025

State general fund 64% · Host towns 36%

The state budget ended the equity and addiction shares. Host money goes to each town with a dispensary, for any lawful purpose.

**Liberty Twp** Moratorium still in place

**Sources and notes for this part**

Yearly sales are the change in the state's cumulative weekly totals. 2026 runs through the week ending Sept 19. Depending on where the year's weeks are cut, 2025 adult use was $829M or $836M; the chart uses the calendar-week cut for both markets. The state's Oct 2 summary sheet repeats the adult-use figures in its medical and total columns, so this page uses the weekly spreadsheet. Statewide tax collected isn't published in a primary source; 10% of adult-use sales since launch would be roughly $192 million, an estimate, not an official figure. Host payments are from the first distribution on Jan 7, 2026, as reported by the Journal-News. Butler County dispensaries were matched to the state list by address and are approximate. Statewide, an Ohio State law school tracker counts 224 places with moratoriums as of Oct 1, 2026, and says the list may be incomplete.
